question: Has the corrected orchestrator surfaced a REAL scheduled failure as a failure, rather than reporting it green?
verdict: PROVEN — a natural production failure propagated non-zero and alerted. Nothing was forced.

propagation: the Python settler raised and exited non-zero
automation_settle.sh reported '✗ MLB settlement FAILED' and '· mlb step: FAILED' rather than a success line
the step ended with '##[error]Process completed with exit code 2'
the health gate aborted publish rather than deploying a broken slate
the notify step raised '##[error]GameTimePicks nightly-settle: workflow FAILED on main'

whyThisIsTheProofAndNotAnAccident: Sprint 049 found automation_settle.sh reporting a hard integrity refusal as success, because a step written as `$PY -m module 2>&1 | tee log` takes its exit status from tee. `set -o pipefail` was added, and the only evidence available was a deterministic known-negative test. This run is the first time the corrected orchestrator met a genuine production failure: the settler could not find a board that did not exist, and every layer above it — script, step, health gate, alert — reported failure. That is exactly the behaviour the fix was written for, observed on a failure nobody manufactured.

namedLimitation.detail: OPS_WEBHOOK_URL is unset, so the alert was written to the run log rather than delivered to an operator. The failure was surfaced; it was not pushed. Setting that secret is a founder action.
namedLimitation.consequence: a real failure is visible only to whoever opens the Actions tab — which is why this one went unnoticed for two days

relatedFinding: The failure this proves was itself caused by the SAME defect class in a sibling script: automation_projections.sh had no pipefail, so a crashing board generator printed '✓ MLB board generation completed' and went green from 2026-07-29. Fixed in this program, along with automation_refresh.sh, with a guard that sweeps every automation_*.sh.
